cards.text: Moses, Israel's leader, gets a new message from the LORD. It's for Moses' brother Aaron, Aaron's sons and all the Israelites. That's the WHOLE group chat, friend, so nobody gets to say they missed the message.
Here's the first rule, and it's about where. Say someone from the house of Israel slaughters an ox, a lamb or a goat, in the camp or outside of it.

cards.question: God says the ox, lamb or goat has to be brought somewhere to be presented as an offering to the LORD. Where?

answers.text: The entrance to the Tent of Meeting
The banks of the Jordan River

cards.question: God says a man who slaughters the animal without bringing it there has shed blood and must be cut off from his people.
God says the Israelites will now bring the LORD the sacrifices they've been offering somewhere else. Where have they been offering them?

cards.text: Now they bring them to the priest at the entrance, as peace offerings. The priest splatters the blood on the LORD's altar and burns the fat as a pleasing aroma to the LORD, and friend, I've chased a pleasing aroma my WHOLE life and the best I ever did was a kitchen that smelled like chocolate chips.

cards.question: Then God names what has to stop. Who must the Israelites no longer offer their sacrifices to?
God says this rule about where to bring sacrifices only lasts as long as Moses leads Israel.

cards.text: Then God adds burnt offerings and every other sacrifice. Same deal: if it doesn't come to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, that man is cut off from his people.

cards.question: The rule about bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Tent of Meeting also covers foreigners living among the Israelites.

cards.text: Now God turns to blood. If anyone eats any blood, Israelite or foreigner, God says, "I will set My face against that person and cut him off from among his people." Friend, when the God who made everything says that, you do NOT want to be that person.

cards.question: Then God explains why eating blood is off-limits. What reason does He give?

answers.text: The life of the flesh is in the blood
Blood is set aside for the priests alone
Blood spreads sickness through the camp

cards.question: God says He has given the Israelites the blood for a purpose on the altar. What is it?

answers.text: To make atonement for their souls
To mark the borders of their camp
To seal their treaties with other nations

cards.text: So God says it again: no Israelite and no foreigner living among them may eat blood. Then He gets to hunting, when someone brings down a wild animal or bird that may be eaten.

cards.question: What must the hunter do with the blood of the wild animal or bird he brings down?

answers.text: Drain it and cover it with dirt

cards.question: God's rule against eating blood only covers oxen, lambs and goats.

cards.text: Then a different case. Someone, native or foreigner, eats an animal found dead or mauled by wild beasts, so he has to wash his clothes and bathe with water.

cards.question: After he washes his clothes and bathes, how long is the person who ate the dead animal unclean?
And if that person skips washing his clothes and bathing, what happens?

answers.text: He owes the priest a goat
He must sleep outside the camp

cards.text: That's the end of this message, friend. But trust me, the LORD's not done talking to Moses, so keep that apron on.

findings.problem: This story card packs more than two beats: the people bring the offerings to the priest, the priest splatters the blood on the altar, the priest burns the fat, and then a long joke is attached with 'and friend.' It needs to be split.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'Now God turns to blood.', the retold law with its quote, and the 'Friend, when the God who made everything…' line. Only the opening card may run to three sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'The life of the flesh is in the blood,' is the only one that sounds like Bible wording. The wrong answers sound plain and modern ('Blood spreads sickness through the camp'), so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'Blood is set aside for the priests alone' could be argued from the passage. The priest is the one who splatters the blood on the altar (Lev 17:6), and God says He gave the blood for the altar (Lev 17:11). A baker could reasonably claim it is right.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The stop has 8 multiple choice cards, 4 true or false cards and no fill in the blank cards. Multiple choice dominates the stop by a wide margin.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: The voice is mostly pleasant rather than laugh-out-loud funny. Only cards 1, 6 and 11 try for a laugh. Card 11's 'you do NOT want to be that person' reads like a nice dad's warning. Cards 9, 14 and 17 are flat retelling where a reaction or comparison could carry a real laugh without muddying the facts.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: The whole passage is rules for sacrifices and for blood. The long-stretch rule lists 'rules for offerings and feasts' as a long stretch that gets one summary card and no choice cards. The same section says 'key laws' are not a long stretch. The walkthrough treats the whole passage as key law and asks about it card by card.
findings.question: When an entire passage (here, a Sermons passage) is made of offering rules, should it be treated as key laws and get choice cards, or does the long-stretch rule apply to part or all of it?

findings.problem: Card 1 says Aaron is Moses' brother. That fact comes from outside the passage (for example, Exodus 4:14), but the card cites only Leviticus 17:1-2. The docs say outside facts need their reference, but the citation rule says a card cites only the verses it tells, 'no wider and no narrower.' The new-person examples ('Cyrus, king of Persia') also carry no reference.
findings.question: Does a new-person introduction that uses a fact from outside the passage need its own reference? If so, how should it be cited on a story card whose verses field covers only the passage verses it tells?
